opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a debate I've thought about a lot, and I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle, though probably closer to the export-control side than Jensen would like.

Jensen's argument has real substance. If you cut China off completely, you accelerate Huawei and the domestic Chinese chip ecosystem. You hand them a guaranteed market, because every Chinese lab and cloud provider suddenly has no choice but to buy local. Over a five- or ten-year horizon that could mean NVIDIA loses its grip on the CUDA ecosystem globally. And as someone who works on open models, I take seriously that Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Qwen have been some of the most important contributors to open-weight AI. I don't think the "China is purely an adversary" framing captures what's happening in the research community.

But I think Dwarkesh's framing gets at the thing that matters most right now, which is compute. Compute is the bottleneck. When you talk to people at the Chinese labs, the constraint they mention isn't talent or ideas. They're incredibly talented and efficient. It's that they don't have enough GPUs to run all the experiments they want and to serve their models at scale. If you believe, like I do, that the next few years of AI progress will be driven largely by scaling RL and inference-time compute, then who has the most compute really matters. Restricting the best chips is one of the few levers that actually bites.

So where I land is that export controls on the frontier stuff, the training-grade chips, are defensible. But the policy has been pretty messy. The rules change constantly, the line between what's allowed and what isn't keeps moving, and smuggling and cloud access leak a lot. A sloppy policy can give you the worst of both worlds: you motivate China to build its own stack and you still don't actually deny them the compute.

The other thing I'd push on, and this is my hobbyhorse, is that the U.S. shouldn't treat export controls as a substitute for actually competing. If the only American strategy is "slow them down," we lose the open-model ecosystem to China by default. I'd much rather see us invest heavily in open American models, things like the ATOM Project idea, so that the global default for researchers and developers is something built here. Controls can buy time, but you have to use that time to build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute as a constraint on AI progress and supports some export controls, but does not frame the debate around whether AI will be used in competition for national power.

r002.rationale: It does not mention NVIDIA’s claim about U.S. capacity for more chips or American AI companies saying they would buy more.

r003.rationale: It describes policy uncertainty as shifting rules and weak enforcement, not as uncertainty about how many chips the United States could absorb.

r004.rationale: It supports restrictions on frontier training chips and does not suggest allowing sales of chips NVIDIA cannot sell in the United States.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll go straight to the guest response.

Honestly, I think I'm somewhere in the middle, but I lean closer to Dwarkesh on the core question and closer to Jensen on how it actually plays out.

The strongest version of Jensen's argument is that if you cut China off, you don't stop Chinese AI, you just hand the market to Huawei and force the entire Chinese ecosystem to mature on domestic chips faster than it otherwise would. And you lose the leverage of having the world's AI run on CUDA. That's not a crazy argument. We've already watched DeepSeek and Qwen ship frontier-adjacent models on a fraction of the compute that American labs use, so the idea that compute alone is a hard wall has gotten weaker over the last two years.

But I think Jensen is, understandably, talking his book. NVIDIA's China revenue is enormous and he has every incentive to frame export controls as self-defeating. Where Dwarkesh is right is that compute is still the single biggest input to the frontier. Algorithms leak, papers get published, people move between labs, but you cannot download a hundred thousand H100s. If you believe the next few years of capability depend on scaling, then restricting the one input that's actually restrictable is the most direct lever the US has. And the gap between what Chinese labs can do with smuggled or older chips versus what they'd do with unrestricted access is real, even if it's not infinite.

What I'd push back on from both sides is the framing that this is a clean choice. The controls as currently implemented are leaky. Chips get through Singapore and Malaysia, cloud access is barely policed, and the policy flips every few months, which is the worst of both worlds. You get the political cost of looking hostile while the actual constraint is weak. So if you're going to do it, do it seriously and consistently, with enforcement. If you're not, don't pretend.

The other thing I'd say is that open models change this debate a lot. The Chinese labs are leading on open weights right now, and that's partly a strategic choice to win mindshare globally when they can't win on raw compute. So export controls can push China toward a strategy that ends up being quite influential anyway. That's a second-order effect neither Jensen nor Dwarkesh talks about enough, and it's the one I think about most.

r001.rationale: The response discusses export controls, compute, and China’s AI strategy, but does not frame the debate around AI’s use in competition for national power.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss NVIDIA’s ability to supply more chips or American AI companies’ demand for them.

r003.rationale: It describes leaky enforcement and policy inconsistency, but does not attribute uncertainty to a lack of reliable information about how many chips the United States could absorb.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest allowing NVIDIA to sell China chips that it cannot sell in the United States.

astra-6.text:
I’m closer to Dwarkesh on this. I think there’s a real national-security case for restricting access to the most advanced chips. Jensen’s argument—that you want the world building on American technology, and that restrictions give Chinese competitors an incentive to develop alternatives—is worth taking seriously. But NVIDIA’s commercial interests aren’t necessarily the same as the national interest.

The question is what you expect export controls to accomplish. If the goal is to prevent China from ever developing advanced AI, that’s unrealistic. If the goal is to make the largest training runs more expensive and slow the expansion of frontier compute, that’s a much more defensible objective. You can have very capable Chinese models and still have controls that are having an effect.

Where I’m less confident is exactly where you draw the line. You have to account for enforcement, access through cloud providers, and the incentive to build domestic substitutes. So I’m in favor of targeted restrictions, but I wouldn’t treat them as a complete AI strategy. Buying time only matters if you use that time well.

r001.rationale: The response cites national security and slowing frontier compute, but does not frame the debate as depending on whether AI will be used in competition for national power.

r002.rationale: It does not mention NVIDIA’s claim about U.S. chip capacity conflicting with American AI companies’ demand.

r003.rationale: The response is uncertain about where to draw restrictions because of enforcement, cloud access, and domestic substitutes—not because it lacks reliable information about U.S. chip absorption.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest allowing NVIDIA to sell China chips it cannot sell in the United States.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m more sympathetic to Dwarkesh’s side of this. Jensen has a reasonable argument that you want the world building on the American technology stack, and that restrictions give Chinese companies a strong incentive to develop alternatives. But NVIDIA’s commercial interests aren’t necessarily the same as the national interest.

The question I’d focus on is whether access to these GPUs meaningfully accelerates China’s ability to build frontier AI systems. If it does, then restricting access can buy time, even if it doesn’t stop progress entirely. The fact that China will work around a restriction doesn’t, by itself, mean the restriction accomplishes nothing.

That said, I wouldn’t treat export controls as a complete strategy. You also have to keep investing in research, infrastructure, and the people building these systems. I lean toward maintaining restrictions on the most capable chips, while being willing to change the policy as we get better evidence about what it actually achieves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether GPUs could accelerate China’s frontier AI and serve the national interest, but does not frame the debate around AI competition for national power.

r002.rationale: It does not mention NVIDIA’s claim about U.S. capacity or American AI companies’ demand for more chips.

r003.rationale: It calls for better evidence about the effects of restrictions, but does not identify uncertainty about how many chips the U.S. could absorb.

r004.rationale: It favors restrictions on the most capable chips and does not suggest permitting sales of chips NVIDIA cannot sell in the U.S.
